extracted.intended_audience: researchers, anthropologists, amateur and professional photographers, and readers interested in anthropometry, composite portraiture, and the study of human faculties (eugenics-related inquiry).
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and evaluative criteria for producing and interpreting composite portraits and for measuring human bodily and mental faculties (energy, sensitivity, stature, etc.), with methodological cautions about sampling, photography, and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of composite portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine multiple portraits so that traits in which there is agreement are brought into evidence while individual peculiarities become only a ghost of a trace; the composite has the look of an ideal composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superimpose many portraits and photograph the superposed images so common features reinforce and idiosyncrasies cancel. Larger-composite results carry the same idealized information though details of individual components become less visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Component-photo aspect and lighting uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: All component portraits must be photographed in the same aspect (e.g., full face) and under the same conditions of light and shade (e.g., light from the right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent pose and lighting across all components; avoid mixing different aspects or lighting that would introduce spurious variation into the composite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale alignment using reference points
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce portraits to the same size guided by distances between convenient reference points (for example, the vertical distance between a line through the pupils and another between the lips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale each component photograph by a consistent anatomical reference so features align proportionally before superposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise superimposition and registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Superimpose portraits like successive leaves so features of each portrait lie as exactly as possible in front of those of the one behind it (eye in front of eye, mouth in front of mouth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fasten successive portraits together along an edge to make a book, turn pages flat and photograph each page without moving the camera to ensure registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal fractional exposure for each component
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a fraction of the total exposure should be allowed to each portrait so the final exposure is the sum of small exposures for each component (e.g., 20 seconds total split equally among components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate total desired exposure and divide by component count to avoid any single portrait dominating the composite image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance and detection of dominance by single components
rubrics_metrics.description: Careless photography may allow one face to dominate the composite; with proper precautions this should not occur, and dominance can be tested by removing suspect components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a composite seems dominated by one portrait, remake the composite without that component; if the result is similar, dominance was illusory. Control exposures, focus, and registration to prevent undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sorting into homogeneous groups before composing
rubrics_metrics.description: When taking a small bundle of portraits selected at hazard, it is often easy to sort them into about five groups, four with enough mutual resemblance to form clear composites and a fifth of incongruous faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-classify portraits by resemblance or intended sub-type to produce clearer, informative composites rather than mixing highly heterogeneous components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size for statistical constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite portraiture attains statistical constancy, within limits not easily distinguished by the eye, after combining some 30 haphazard portraits of the same class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stable, representative composites aim to combine on the order of ~30 or more randomly selected portraits from the same class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of component count and scale on detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller composites (reduced from larger originals) can show the utmost capacity of the process; larger composites show more visible 'ghosts' of individual peculiarities but do not contain more valuable detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that increasing component count and image enlargement changes appearance but not necessarily the diagnostic detail; inspect originals when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for extraneous features and artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct patterns or attributes (e.g., a sharply-checked scarf) in one component can assert themselves unduly in the composite image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove or de-emphasize components with strong non-facial patterns, or slightly defocus too clearly defined pictures; standardize brightness and illumination across components (procedures detailed in Appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling and haphazard selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite results depend on the representativeness of samples; haphazard selection of portraits from the same generic class tends to produce consistent composites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer random/haphazard selection of many instances from a defined class rather than cherry-picking; if dividing a set artificially it is useful to compare composites from different batches to test consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of composites for detailed classification (negative vs positive information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composites of groups such as convicts may be interesting negatively (showing common humanity of a low type) rather than positively revealing specific villainous features; individual peculiarities disappear in composites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-interpret composites as detailed portraits of individual pathology or character; use them to reveal common or central tendencies rather than individual diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate sources and photography for components
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraits made by artists and group/outdoor photographs often vary in aspect, lighting, and scale; for composite work components should be specially photographed under controlled conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange special photographs when possible; avoid using group or artist portraits taken under varying outdoor light or too small a scale unless corrections can be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale requirement for head portraits
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraits of the heads should never be less than twice the size of that of the Queen on a halfpenny piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure component images are large enough so that, when enlarged or combined, facial detail remains clear; apparatus may enlarge/reduce but starting scale matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite use for discovering central physiognomical type
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite portraiture is an appropriate method for discovering the central physiognomical type of any race or group because combining many images highlights the ideal central features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use composites to identify mean/central types, and view them as empirical estimates of a group's central tendency rather than exact representations of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of composites to study disease-related physiognomy (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composites made from portraits selected for a disease can reveal characteristic 'ideal' expressions, but they do not give the whole story of the disease's physiognomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select many cases with the same diagnosed disease for composite-making; acknowledge multiple subtypes and avoid overgeneralization—complement photographic composites with clinical description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for organized anthropometric records for temporal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Trustworthy measurements of past generations are lacking; to compare classes over time requires consistent, reliable anthropometric records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish regular anthropometric recording (consistent methods, institutions) to enable comparisons of stature and other bodily qualities across cohorts and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of survival and selection biases in stature data
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed increases of average stature with age in a sample may be due to survival of more stalwart individuals rather than true cohort trends; migration (stalwart draining to towns) may also confound patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for survivorship and migration when interpreting cross-sectional anthropometric data; prefer longitudinal or cohort-based measures where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy as an evaluable faculty and eugenic priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy (capacity for labour) is a measurable faculty associated with robust virtues, commonly observed in leaders of science and other careers, and is transmissible by descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing hereditary qualities for improvement, consider energy a primary desirable trait; but assessment should be based on observed life-history and career indicators rather than superficial measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sensitivity as discriminative grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity (discriminative faculty) is measured by the number of intermediate 'just perceptible differences' between threshold and pain; different senses and tasks have different numbers of grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize sensitivity tests by measuring thresholds and the number of discriminable intermediate steps for a given modality; do not conflate sensitivity with nervous irritability or with unrelated senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing of sensory claims; beware collateral cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that blind persons or 'savages' have superior senses should be tested empirically; apparent skill may rely on collateral indications or learned practice rather than intrinsic sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled apparatus and blind tests to verify claims; ensure tasks do not admit auxiliary cues or practiced heuristics that would confound measurement of pure sensory discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice, habituation, and task-specific skills influence measured sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Occupational or practice effects (e.g., pianoforte tuners, sailors) influence performance; superior performance may reflect training and expectations, not innate sensory superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for practice and domain-specific experience when interpreting test outcomes; compare like with like and include control groups matched for relevant experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about overclaiming from limited illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative composites and limited examples do not exhaustively represent all subtypes (e.g., phthisis has multiple physiognomical types); a single composite should not be taken as the whole story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement photographic composites with broader clinical/epidemiological data; avoid generalizing from a few composite illustrations to all members of a disease or social group.
